title: On‑Prem network policy chaos — incident notes and runbook draft
body:
Summary:
During a scheduled customer onboarding (acme-inc on-prem bundle) we observed intermittent loss of control-plane connectivity for their private deployment. Symptoms: API calls to the control-plane timed out from customer nodes for short windows (~30–120s). Control-plane itself reported healthy from our side; customer metrics showed repeated TCP handshakes failing and then recovering.

Impact:
- Affected: control-plane API calls (model fetch, liveliness checks) on 6 out of 12 worker nodes for ~4 hours with repeated short outages.
- Customer-visible: occasional request errors and increased latency for management operations; no user data lost.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2026-03-09 02:18 — First Pager: synthetic health-checks for acme-inc failing (alert threshold 3m).
- 2026-03-09 02:25 — Oncall (Aisha) triage: customer reported same on Slack; customer engineer mentions they were applying updated egress policies.
- 2026-03-09 02:33 — SREs requested tcpdump from one affected node; customer uploaded capture at 02:37.
- 2026-03-09 02:40 — Observed SYN packets reaching control-plane but no SYN-ACK returned at times; in other traces control-plane SYN-ACK present but client did not accept (RST from network).
- 2026-03-09 03:10 — Hypothesis shifted to asymmetric routing/SNAT issue or firewall state table limit.
- 2026-03-09 04:05 — Customer reverted recent egress-policy patch; incidents subsided but flaps continued intermittently.
- 2026-03-09 05:30 — Temporary mitigation: customer added explicit allow rules for control-plane source CIDRs and opened health-check port range; connectivity stabilized.

Diagnostics performed (commands and observations):
- ss -tanp on node: showed many connections in SYN_RECV and a handful of RSTs.
- sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 port 443 and host <control-plane-ip>: captured SYNs from customer nodes and sporadic ICMP fragmentation-needed messages.
- iptables -S / nft list ruleset on nodes: customer had MASQUERADE rule for outbound with --to-source set for SNAT; few odd ACCEPT/REJECT entries ordered earlier than NAT rules.
- ip route show / ip rule: multiple policy routes; asymmetric egress path present when traffic left through secondary transit link.
- kernel logs: occasional nf_conntrack: table full: failed to create conntrack entry.

Root cause analysis (working hypothesis):
1) Customer rolled out a tightened egress policy that inadvertently changed the SNAT ordering and introduced asymmetric routing for control-plane health traffic. Two contributing factors: (a) conntrack table on their edge firewall was reaching capacity (stateful device), causing some established state to be dropped and then later causing RST behavior; (b) an MTU reduction on the transit link caused TCP handshake fragmentation/ICMP messages leading to sporadic failure of TLS handshakes.
2) The combination produced intermittent failures rather than full outage because some nodes used a different egress path or reused existing conntrack entries.

Why this wasn't caught earlier:
- Our onboarding checklist requested ports/ips but did not explicitly require ephemeral port allowances for stateful health checks or note conntrack sizing guidance.
- No automated e2e test exercising control-plane handshakes under reduced conntrack capacity or MTU mismatch was in the onboarding test harness.

Immediate mitigation steps taken:
- Asked customer to revert the egress policy change (they did partially).
- Customer increased conntrack table sizes on their firewall and edge NAT for the transit device.
- Temporary allow rule added for control-plane CIDR + health ports and ephemeral port range (49152–65535) from worker subnets.
- Adjusted our client keepalive to slightly longer TTLs to reduce new connection churn during reconnection windows.

Workaround and recovery notes for oncall (runbook draft snippet):
- Detection:
  - If control-plane health alerts for on-prem deployment fire, check for: increased SYN_RECV, RST count, icmp fragmentation-needed messages.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Run: sudo ss -untap | grep <control-plane-ip> — confirm SYN/SYN_RECV/RST patterns.
  2) Request tcpdump from customer: sudo tcpdump -n -i <iface> host <control-plane-ip> and upload capture.
  3) Check kernel conntrack: sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count and net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max. If count close to max -> ask customer to bump nf_conntrack_max and monitor.
  4) Check firewall/NAT rules ordering: ask customer to show iptables -t nat -S and ensure MASQUERADE/POSTROUTING not preempted by REJECT rules.
  5) Run: tracepath <control-plane-ip> to check MTU path and look for pmtu reductions.
- Temporary fixes to suggest to customer:
  - Increase conntrack table, or reduce conntrack timeout for short-lived flows.
  - Add explicit allow for control-plane CIDRs + ephemeral port range in stateful firewall to avoid asymmetric drops.
  - If using dual transit links, add symmetric routing or source-based routing to keep replies on same path.

Permanent remediation & follow-ups (action items):
- [ACTIONS] Update onboarding network checklist to require: explicit ephemeral port guidance, conntrack sizing recommendations, MTU validation steps. Owner: Priya Menon. Due: 2026-03-19.
- [ACTIONS] Add e2e test to private-deploy test harness: simulate conntrack saturation and MTU reduction to validate client handshake resilience. Owner: Marco Ruiz. Due: 2026-04-02.
- [ACTIONS] Create a short customer-facing KB: "Private deployment network checklist — stateful firewalls and NAT" including example iptables/nft commands, throughput hints, and tcpdump snippets. Owner: Evelyn Zhang. Due: 2026-03-22.
- [ACTIONS] Revise runbook (this doc) into formal playbook with step-by-step commands and canned messages for customers. Owner: Aisha Patel. Due: 2026-03-16.

Runbook draft — canned commands to share with customer (copy/paste):
- tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 host <CONTROL_PLANE_IP> and save to /tmp/cp.pcap
- conntrack check: sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count && sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
- increase conntrack: sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144
- show NAT rules: sudo iptables -t nat -S || sudo nft list table nat
- check MTU path: tracepath <CONTROL_PLANE_IP>

Post-incident notes:
- Customer was cooperative and reverted change quickly once we showed tcpdump evidence; collaboration was good and no SLA breach.
- Log snippets and pcap attached to JIRA-6572 (see linked artifacts).
- Consider providing a small network-validation tool in the agent bundle that runs these checks automatically during onboarding.

Open questions:
- Do we want to require customers to allow a fixed ephemeral port range, or is recommending conntrack sizing sufficient?
- Should we modify the agent to optionally use a persistent TCP connection for control-plane health to reduce handshake churn?

References and attachments:
- attached: pcap from 2026-03-09 02:37 (JIRA-6572)
- onboarding checklist (current): CONFLUENCE:Private-Deployments-Network-Requirements

Notes to self / rough ideas to polish into the final runbook:
- Short checklist for SREs: check conntrack -> request pcap -> recommend immediate allow rule -> escalate to network eng if asymmetric routing suspected.
- Include diagrams: expected symmetric path vs observed asymmetric case (draw in Confluence).
- Add a small script for customers to collect all required artifacts (ss, iptables, tracepath, tcpdump) and upload to support bundle.

Document history:
- 2026-03-09 initial incident capture and triage notes (Aisha)
- 2026-03-10 root cause hypothesis refined (Marco)
- 2026-03-12 runbook draft and action items added (Aisha, Evelyn)

End of notes.
